title: Slot-fracture reuse sampling and NVMe coalescing diary
content:
Background:

We keep seeing mid-tail latency blips correlated with small groups of keys that repeatedly get evicted/repopulated across slots (what I'm calling 'slot fracture'). These fragments are cheap individually but collectively hammer NVMe read amplification and break batching. Traditional per-key reuse metrics hide the phenomenon because the reuse is high in aggregate but oscillatory at the slot/granularity boundary.

Objective:
- Define a measurable slot-fracture metric that correlates with NVMe read amplification and tail latency.
- Design a sampling-based runtime probe to estimate slot-fracture without full trace capture.
- Prototype NVMe coalescing heuristics that reduce read amplification from fractured hotsets.

Hypotheses:
1) Slot-fracture can be detected by tracking short-lived residency toggles per stripe/slot: the more toggles per second, the higher the effective read amplification.
2) Simple time-windowed coalescing (delay small reads up to X ms to accumulate adjacent page reads) will reduce NVMe IOps and lower p99+ latency at the cost of modest p50 increases for a tiny fraction of requests.
3) Sampling at 0.5% of requests with targeted TTL sketches is enough to surface fracture hotspots with <5% error.

Definitions / metrics we used:
- slot: allocation unit inside our resident-set map (variable sized; in this experiment a slot = 4KB page mapped to a KV segment).
- fracture_toggle: a transition where a slot is evicted and then repopulated within a short window (T_fract).
- toggle_rate: toggles per slot per second over sampling window.
- fracture_index: population-weighted sum(toggle_rate) across slots normalized by active-resident-set.
- read_amplification_ratio: total NVMe reads / logical cache-miss events.
- p50/p95/p99 generation latency and NVMe queue depth distribution.

Experiment design:
- Cluster: dev-infer-4 (4xA100), NVMe: 3x1.6TB on local host (standard config for Dedicated preview).
- Workloads: three synthetic traces derived from production logs (chat-short, multi-turn assistant, long-context retrieval). Each trace contains ~200k requests over 30 minutes.
- Baselines: current LRU-ish eviction with per-slot LRU timestamp; no coalescing; full instrumentation.
- Probes: 0.5% sample of requests record: slot id, evict/pop cycles, seqlen, model variant, latency, NVMe read size. Sampler uses reservoir + TTL sketch to avoid high mem overhead.

Sampling algorithm (sketch):
- On cache miss, with probability p=0.005 mark event for sampling.
- For sampled slots, increment toggle counter if slot was evicted < T_fract (set to 800ms initially) before repopulation.
- Maintain circular window buckets (10s window, 1s resolution) per host and aggregate across GPU workers every 30s.

NVMe coalescing heuristic (prototype):
- For small reads (<32KB) originating from the same logical stripe within 10ms, coalesce into a single NVMe multi-range read (when supported) or an adjacent prefetch read (read up to 128KB aligned to 64KB boundary).
- Delay policy: hold eligible small read up to max_coalesce_delay (default 6ms). If queue grows or read count < threshold, issue immediately.
- Backpressure: if NVMe queue depth > Q_high (empirically 64), bypass coalescing to avoid increasing tail latency.

Key results (summary):
- Sampling: 0.5% rate with our TTL sketch identified top-20 fractured slots with 4.2% false positive and 3.6% false negative vs full-trace ground truth (acceptable for targeted mitigation).
- Toggle signal correlated strongly with read_amplification_ratio (Pearson r=0.78).
- NVMe coalescing reduced small-read NVMe IOps by ~28% and read_amplification_ratio by 19% on chat-short trace.
- Tail latency improvements: p99 generation latency reduced by 12% on chat-short, 7% on multi-turn, negligible on long-context (where big sequential reads dominate).
- p50 increased ~1.3% in coalesced runs (within SLA).
- Worst-case: improper coalescing parameters increased p99 in a stress synthetic scenario (very bursty concurrent small reads) by up to 22% when delay set to 20ms. This drove the inclusion of adaptive delay and NVMe queue-aware bypass.

Observations / field notes:
- Many fracture hotspots live on stripe boundaries. When we aligned prefetch to 64KB boundaries, fragmentation effects dropped.
- Prefetching more aggressively helps but can increase background NVMe bandwidth; we need to tie prefetch aggressiveness to measured read_amplification_ratio and overall system BW headroom.
- The slot id entropy sometimes hid logical affinity (application-level keys that are frequently accessed together but map to different slots). A complementary application-aware coalescing (group by request grouping metadata) would help but requires integration with higher-level routing.
- Sampling artifacts: reservoir approach biases toward initially hot slots. TTL sketch reduces that but tuning TTL is workload-dependent.

Actionable next steps:
1) Land lightweight fracture probe in Canary image (feature flag gated). Keep default sampling p=0.005, TTL 45s. Observe 2 weeks across production-like traffic.
2) Implement adaptive coalescer: delay = min(6ms, 0.1 * measured inter-arrival median for stripe), NVMe-Q-aware bypass. Conservative rollout behind opt-in flag for Dedicated tenants.
3) Add a dashboard tile: fracture_index, small-read IOps trend, read_amplification_ratio, NVMe queue depth. Correlate with p99 latency.
4) Run cross-tenant experiment to measure multi-tenant interference (we suspect tenants with small hotkey churn amplify each other).
5) Explore app-level affinity hints: add optional header for client SDKs to attach grouping tokens to requests to allow coalescing at higher semantic level.

Open questions / uncertainties:
- Optimal T_fract: 800ms worked for our testbed but might vary with model seqlen distribution; we should autosuggest based on seqlen histogram and NVMe latencies.
- Is prefetching to 128KB universally safe? Some tenants are bandwidth-sensitive; need per-tenant config or global cost accounting.
- Interaction with KV cache eviction policies that already use aging + frequency: do we double-count and thus evict incorrectly? Need a simulation run on full production traces.

Notes to self (TODO):
- Add unit tests for sampler to verify unbiasedness over long tails.
- Draft a short RFC for the coalescer feature flag and rollout plan (include safe kill-switch).
- Share initial Canary metrics with Solutions Eng for Dedicated pilot tenants next Wednesday.

Appendix (experiment logs excerpts):
- 2026-02-18 10:02: sample-run-1: chat-short, p99 gen latency: baseline 184ms -> coalesced 162ms, NVMe IOps small-read 3.8k -> 2.7k
- 2026-02-21 14:55: burst-stress-variant: coalescing delay 20ms -> p99 spike +22% (rollback)
- 2026-03-02 09:10: multi-tenant dry run: fracture_index correlated with tenant-CPU steal events (interesting!)

References / links: see linked_artifacts above.

Questions for reviewers:
- Are we comfortable defaulting sample p to 0.5% in Canary? The memory overhead is ~8MB/host with TTL sketch.
- Any legal/ops concerns for per-request grouping headers (privacy)? Marking for Security review.

-- Aisha
